system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Classic stiff-person syndrome is an autoimmune CNS disorder characterized by fluctuating axial and proximal-limb rigidity and painful spasms triggered by sensory or emotional stimuli; high-titer anti-GAD65 antibodies are common and reflect association with impaired inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission.
vignette: A 44-year-old woman has 18 months of progressive stiffness of the trunk and proximal legs. Sudden noises and emotional stress trigger painful whole-body spasms. Examination shows marked lumbar hyperlordosis and rigid paraspinal muscles. Electromyography shows continuous motor-unit activity at rest. Serum anti-GAD65 antibody titer is markedly elevated.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Tetanus causes acute toxin-mediated disinhibition with trismus and autonomic instability after a wound; this chronic autoimmune pattern with anti-GAD65 and continuous axial rigidity is different.
Isaacs syndrome is a peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder with myokymia/neuromyotonia rather than the classic stimulus-triggered axial rigidity of stiff-person syndrome.
Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, resting tremor, and extrapyramidal rigidity rather than painful stimulus-triggered spasms with anti-GAD65 antibodies.
Myotonic dystrophy causes myotonia, weakness, cataracts, and systemic features, not this autoimmune axial-rigidity syndrome.
key_expl: Progressive axial rigidity, stimulus-triggered painful spasms, continuous motor-unit activity, and a high anti-GAD65 titer identify classic stiff-person syndrome.
objective: Diagnose stiff-person syndrome from chronic axial/proximal rigidity, stimulus-triggered spasms, continuous motor activity, and anti-GAD65 autoimmunity.
clues: painful spasms triggered by noise or stress
